_about: Physiological parameters for Dichromascope. Source of truth: tools/sync_species.py copies the numeric values into index.html and lab.html. Grades: A = measured in this species, several animals, modern method; B = measured but few animals, older or indirect; C = derived from measured quantities via the model; D = assumed or borrowed from another species. See docs/parameters.md and docs/species/*.md for derivations and references.

colour_vision_limit_cd_m2.source: Roth, Balkenius & Kelber 2008 (humans tested in the horse apparatus)

brightness_weber_fraction_task_matched.source: Value cited by Griebel and colleagues (2004) for humans in comparable grey-card tasks; original source not checked

lambda_S_nm.source: Guenther & Zrenner 1993; ganglion-cell spectral sensitivity, 450 nm S-cone input

lambda_L_nm.source: Guenther & Zrenner 1993 (550 nm); Crocker et al. 1980 (556 nm)

lens_cutoff_nm.source: Assumed; only affects wavelengths below ~400 nm

S_cone_fraction.source: Linberg et al. 2001: M/L cones 80-90% of cones

weber_luminance.source: No large-field brightness Weber fraction found for cats; borrowed from dog (Griebel and colleagues 2004)

weber_chromatic_L.source: Conventional receptor-noise default (Vorobyev & Osorio 1998 lineage); not measured in cats

colour_limit_cd_m2.source: Assumed equal to horse and human (Roth et al. 2008)

neutral_point_nm.note: Cat colour discrimination needs stimuli >~20 deg (Loop & Bruce 1978; Loop, Bruce & Petuchowski 1979); no neutral-point measurement found

lambda_R_nm.source: Guenther & Zrenner 1993 (dark-adapted ganglion cells peak at 501 nm)

rod_sensitivity_vs_cones.source: Human rods ~1000x more sensitive than cones (scotopic vs cone threshold); cats ~0.74 log units more sensitive than humans in dim light (Kang et al. 2009), so x5

rod_weber_ratio.source: Rod luminance Weber fraction assumed 3x the cone value; human rods follow a shallower, noisier increment-threshold curve (Sharpe et al. 1989, 1992)

rod_saturation_cd_m2.source: Order of magnitude from human rod increment saturation (Aguilar & Stiles 1954)

lambda_S_nm.source: Neitz, Geist & Jacobs 1989; Jacobs et al. 1993 (430-435 nm)

lambda_L_nm.source: Neitz, Geist & Jacobs 1989; Jacobs et al. 1993

S_cone_fraction.source: Mowat et al. 2008: 9.9-11.9% in area centralis, 15-18% inferior periphery

weber_luminance.source: Griebel and colleagues 2004, J. Vision 4(3):10; three dogs

weber_chromatic_L.source: Conventional receptor-noise default; not measured in dogs

colour_limit_cd_m2.source: Assumed equal to horse and human (Roth et al. 2008)

lambda_R_nm.source: Jacobs et al. 1993 (dog rod pigment ~508 nm)

rod_weber_ratio.source: Rod luminance Weber fraction assumed 3x the cone value; human rods follow a shallower, noisier increment-threshold curve (Sharpe et al. 1989, 1992)

rod_saturation_cd_m2.source: Order of magnitude from human rod increment saturation (Aguilar & Stiles 1954)

S_cone_fraction.source: Sandmann et al. 1996: S cones 10-25% depending on location

weber_luminance.source: Geisbauer et al. 2004; two horses. Consistent with Macuda & Timney 1999 (chance below ~0.2 log units)

weber_chromatic_L.source: Conventional receptor-noise default; not measured in horses

colour_limit_cd_m2.source: Roth, Balkenius & Kelber 2008; two horses, humans 0.02 in same apparatus

lambda_R_nm.source: No horse measurement found; mammalian rhodopsin is ~500 nm with little variation
